title: Accents, background noise, and bad connections on calls
seoTitle: Accents, background noise, and bad call handling | ROAL
description: Handle accents, background noise, and weak connections on restaurant calls with better scripts, setup tips, and fallback steps.
question: How do I handle accents, background noise, and bad connections on AI phone calls for my restaurant?
answer: The fix is to make the phone host speak plainly, confirm key order details, and give callers an easy way to repeat or slow down when the line is noisy. In a restaurant, the best setup also includes a clear menu source, a fallback to staff for tricky calls, and call forwarding that routes busy or unanswered calls correctly.
summary: You’ll know how to reduce call confusion and set up practical backup steps for noisy or hard-to-hear restaurant calls.
intro:
Accents, background noise, and bad connections can make any phone call messy. For a restaurant, the answer is not to hope callers speak perfectly. It is to set clear phone rules, use simple confirmation steps, and send hard calls to staff when needed.

An AI phone host can help with that if it is trained on your menu, hours, and order flow. ROAL answers restaurant calls, takes pickup and delivery orders, and sends a clean ticket to the kitchen screen. It also has a clear handoff path for questions it cannot settle on the spot.

sections.h2: Why do accents and noisy calls cause mistakes on restaurant orders?
sections.body:
Restaurant calls are hard because people speak fast, orders have names that sound alike, and kitchens are loud. Add a thick accent, a noisy dining room, or a weak signal, and you get the kind of call where one word can change the whole order.

The fix starts with how the host listens and confirms. A good phone host should not try to guess. It should ask short follow-up questions and repeat the order in plain language. For example: "I heard one large pepperoni and one small cheese. Is that right?" That one sentence can catch a lot of errors before they reach the kitchen.

A practical restaurant checklist:
- Keep menu names simple where possible.
- Use the same words on the phone that appear on the menu.
- Ask for size, toppings, and any note one by one.
- Repeat back the final order before sending it.
- Move complex calls to staff when the caller sounds unsure.

ROAL is built to read the live menu, sizes, modifiers, and notes from your restaurant setup, then confirm the order back before it sends the ticket. That helps when the line is noisy or the caller speaks with a strong accent, because the host can slow the flow down and ask for clarification instead of rushing.

sections.h2: What should an AI phone host say when the line is noisy?
sections.body:
When the call has static, echo, a child in the background, or kitchen noise, the host should use short phrases and one question at a time. Long explanations make bad audio worse.

Use a simple call flow like this:
1. Greet the caller.
2. Ask what they want to order.
3. Confirm items one by one.
4. Ask for pickup or delivery.
5. Collect the name and phone number.
6. Repeat the full order and ready time.

A useful script line is: "No problem, I’ll go one item at a time so I get it right." That sets expectations and often calms the call down.

Here is a small example you can swap for your own menu:

| Step | Example wording |
|---|---|
| Item | "Is that a large meat pizza?" |
| Modifier | "Would you like onions on that?" |
| Note | "Any special instructions for the kitchen?" |
| Contact | "What name should I put on the order?" |
| Repeat back | "So that is one large meat pizza with onions, pickup at 20 minutes." |

This style works well for takeout counters, pizza shops, delis, and family restaurants. It gives the caller room to correct the order before it becomes a ticket.

sections.h2: How do I help callers with strong accents without slowing service?
sections.body:
You do not need to "fix" accents. You need a phone process that handles them fairly and clearly. The best move is to make the call easier for both sides by using shorter questions, fewer choices at once, and a calm pace.

Try these phrases:
- "Take your time."
- "I’ll ask one thing at a time."
- "Please say the size first, then the toppings."
- "If I miss something, I’ll repeat it back."

For a restaurant, the real win is consistency. A caller with a strong accent should get the same order flow as anyone else. That means no fast talk, no jargon, and no guessing. If the host cannot understand a question about a special allergy request or a catering detail, it should not improvise. It should pass the call to staff with a short summary.

ROAL can speak the caller’s language and handle order-taking, hours, address, parking, and menu questions from the restaurant’s public information. If the caller asks something tricky, the question lands in an inbox so the owner can answer it once and the host knows it from then on. That is useful when the same hard question keeps coming up from different callers.

sections.h2: What should I do when the connection is bad or the caller drops out?
sections.body:
Bad connections happen. The caller may be on a cell phone in a parking lot, driving, or standing in a noisy doorway. Your phone host should have a backup plan so the order does not disappear with the call.

A practical backup plan:
- Ask the caller to repeat only the missing part, not the whole order.
- Confirm the phone number before the call ends.
- If the line cuts out, save what you have and ask staff to review it.
- For important calls, hand off anything unclear to the team.

Example script line: "Your line cut out. I have the pizza and salad. Please repeat the drink if you want one." That is better than restarting from zero.

If you use call forwarding, set it up carefully and test it. On many landlines and some carriers, dial *72 and then the forwarding number to forward all calls, and *73 to turn it off. On GSM mobile carriers, **21*number# often forwards all calls and ##21# turns it off; **61*number# often forwards unanswered calls and **67*number# often forwards busy calls. Verizon Wireless uses *72 / *73, and *71 for busy/no-answer forwarding. Business VoIP systems usually handle forwarding in the web portal. Codes vary by carrier and plan, so always confirm with your carrier and test with a real call.

If you want a quick reference, keep [call forwarding codes by carrier](/tools/call-forwarding-codes) bookmarked for the person who handles phones at your shop.

sections.h2: How can I set up an AI phone host so it handles rough calls better?
sections.body:
A solid setup matters as much as the script. The host should know your menu, hours, address, and any common order questions before it answers the phone. That way it spends less time guessing and more time confirming.

A good setup process for a busy restaurant:
1. Paste your website, Google Maps link, or name and city at /try.
2. Check that the host read your menu and prices correctly.
3. Test-call it in the browser and listen for how it handles fast speech.
4. Add menu items, sold-out items, FAQs, and hours if needed.
5. Claim the host and forward your existing number when you are ready.

ROAL reads public pages like website menus, menu PDFs, and menu photos, then builds a phone host in about two minutes. The owner can test-call it without signing up first. After that, the restaurant can forward all calls, or only busy and unanswered calls, and turn forwarding off any time.

A quick owner checklist before going live:
- Spell hard-to-pronounce menu items the way staff say them.
- Mark sold-out items so they are not offered.
- Add common questions about parking, delivery area, or pickup entrance.
- Make sure reservation requests and catering calls go to staff when needed.

If you run multiple locations, keep each location’s hours and menu separate. That prevents a caller from getting the wrong address when the line is busy.

takeaways: Use short questions and repeat key order details to reduce mistakes on noisy calls.
If a call is hard to hear, confirm only the missing part instead of restarting the order.
Set up forwarding carefully and test it with real calls before relying on it.
Send allergy, catering, complaint, and manager requests to staff with a summary.
ROAL can take orders, speak the caller’s language, and pass tricky questions to the team.

faq.q: How should an AI phone host handle callers with strong accents?
faq.a: It should use short questions, one at a time, and repeat the order back in plain language. It should not guess at names, sizes, or toppings. If the host still cannot understand a key detail, it should hand the call to staff with a summary.

faq.q: What should my restaurant do about background noise on phone orders?
faq.a: Use a slower call flow and confirm each part of the order separately. A line like, "I’ll go one item at a time so I get it right," helps a lot. For especially noisy or unclear calls, the host should escalate to staff rather than risk a bad ticket.

faq.q: Can an AI phone host take payment card numbers over the phone?
faq.a: ROAL does not take card numbers over the phone. Payment happens at pickup or however the restaurant already takes it. That keeps the order flow focused on items, name, phone number, and ready time.

faq.q: How do I forward my restaurant number to an AI phone host?
faq.a: You can forward your existing number to the host line, either for all calls or only when busy or unanswered, depending on your carrier and phone system. On many systems there are star codes or a web portal for setup, but codes vary by carrier and plan, so confirm with your provider and test the call before relying on it.
